Where is New Orleans, and what should a seller know about the ground it sits on?

New Orleans is the seat of Orleans Parish, and the city and the parish share the same boundaries. It was founded in the spring of 1718 by the French Mississippi Company under Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville and was named for the Duke of Orleans, then regent of France (Wikipedia).

The ground is the main thing that sets a house here apart from a house in most other cities. The average elevation of the city is between 1 and 2 feet below sea level. Parts of Uptown reach about 20 feet at the base of the river levee, while the far reaches of Eastern New Orleans sit as low as 7 feet below sea level. Levees and drainage pumps hold the water back.

Hurricane Katrina in August 2005 flooded more than 80 percent of the city. Buyers and insurers remember that, so a seller's address, lot elevation and flood history all show up early in any conversation about price and timing.

Which New Orleans facts come up most when a house goes on the market?

Six facts tend to decide how smoothly a New Orleans sale goes: the street's elevation, the condition of the roof and foundation, open code cases, recorded liens, rental history and the tax bill. The table below pulls together the sourced numbers that matter for the paperwork side.

Fee schedules change, so call or check the clerk's site before closing day rather than relying on any table, ours included.

How are sales recorded in Orleans Parish?

Every sale of New Orleans real estate is recorded with the Clerk of Civil District Court in its Land Records Division. State law requires that office to preserve forever the property records filed in Orleans Parish and make them available to the public, per the clerk's fee page.

The clerk's home page notes that the old separate filing fees for mortgages, conveyances and notarial archives have been replaced by a single recording fee. The clerk's fee sheet lists the current amounts, and checks are made payable to the Clerk of Court.

What is the New Orleans documentary transaction tax?

It is a city tax collected by the Notarial Archives on documents that transfer real estate. The clerk's documentary tax page says it applies to sales, donations, transfers, mortgages and commercial leases, and that the seller is one of the parties responsible for paying it.

The tax is a flat $325 for most of these documents. It is paid at the time of recording. If it is not, a billing form must be filled out and the tax paid within 30 days, or interest and a $500 penalty are added. The page also says that a single family residence or residential double whose document runs past 25 pages still pays $325 if a notarized statement confirms it is an owner-occupied single family residence or residential double.

A flat tax is easy to budget. The part sellers miss is the deadline, so confirm in writing who is paying it at the closing table.

What happens when a New Orleans house has code enforcement problems?

Open code cases and recorded liens follow the property, not the owner, so they have to be dealt with before or at a sale. The city's Department of Code Enforcement describes its process on its blight process page, and the steps are worth knowing if you inherited a house or lived elsewhere while it sat vacant.

  • Neighbors or inspectors report the property, and a case opens in the city's LAMA system. The target time from complaint to inspection is 30 days.
  • The Hearings Bureau researches title to find every owner and legal interest, then mails and posts a Notice of Noncompliance with a deadline to fix the violations.
  • If the violations are still open, a hearing is set 30 to 45 days after the compliance period. Owners are required to appear or send a representative, and hearing costs can be charged even when the work was finished before the date.
  • If the owner is found guilty and does not appeal, remediate or pay, a Notice of Judgment is filed with the recorder of mortgages 30 days after the hearing. That filing is a lien and lets the city clean up the property or seize it for sheriff's sale.

The city can cut lots, send a property to sheriff's sale or demolish a building. Sale proceeds first pay liens, taxes and sale costs, and any remainder goes to the former owner.

Can a New Orleans lien be reduced before you sell?

Sometimes. The city runs a Lien Reduction Program for owners who have done significant work to fix violations, but it comes with firm limits.

  • Abatement must be finished before the application, and photos must be dated and time stamped.
  • Liens that were adjudicated or sold at tax sale, liens that were foreclosed on, and paid liens cannot be reduced.
  • Demolition and grass liens can only have interest reduced.
  • Reductions are made per violation, there is no entitlement to one, and there are no appeals. The goal is a response within 30 days.
  • If you pay the lien before the application is processed, the application is denied and the payment is not refunded.

That last rule matters on a closing timeline. Ask the department about a lien payoff and about reduction before the payoff is wired. Forms go to 1340 Poydras Street, Suite 1100, or by email with photos attached, under 25 MB per message.

Does a short term rental history change how a New Orleans house sells?

It can. Short term rentals are not legal in New Orleans without a permit, according to the city's STR overview, and the rules are written in both the municipal code and the Comprehensive Zoning Ordinance. New regulations passed on March 23, 2023 took effect July 1, 2023.

The city's STR administration page says short term rental licenses are not transferable, so a buyer cannot simply take over a seller's permit. The city's application for a residential short term rental owner permit also asks the owner to certify that the dwelling has no outstanding property taxes or city liens on the lot of record.

If you ran an unpermitted rental, the city can send the case to an administrative adjudication hearing, where a hearing officer may impose fines or revoke permits. Clear that history up with the city before you put a closing date on the calendar.

How does the New Orleans property tax bill work at a sale?

The Orleans Parish Assessor sets the assessment and approves exemptions such as the homestead exemption, then certifies the roll to the city Treasurer, who sends the bills. That division of work is laid out on the Treasury's how taxes are calculated page.

For the 2026 tax year the city made bills available online in January 2026, mailed them by the end of that month and gave taxpayers until February 28, 2026 to pay (city announcement). The assessor's number for questions about a valuation is (504) 754-8811. Appeals of a 2026 assessment went to the Board of Review at Delgado Community College's City Park campus between September 15 and October 5, 2025, per the City Council's appeals page.

Closing agents normally prorate the current year's bill between buyer and seller. Ask for a payoff or tax certificate early if the bill is unpaid.

What drives housing demand in New Orleans?

Trade and the port shape the local economy. The Port of New Orleans is the fifth-largest in the United States by cargo volume and the twelfth-largest by cargo value, and the Port of South Louisiana nearby is the world's busiest by bulk tonnage. Wikipedia also notes that the city's economy has always leaned on trade and financial services more than manufacturing. The Census Bureau puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 362,154 residents.

When does selling to a cash buyer make sense in New Orleans?

A cash sale fits best when the problem is the house or the calendar. Common examples here are a vacant inherited house with a code case, a property with a lien the owner cannot finance away, a storm-damaged building that a lender will not appraise, or a rental that lost its permit.

A cash buyer purchases the property as it stands, so there is no appraisal contingency, no lender repair demands and no showings. You still need clear title, so the lien, tax and recording points above apply to every route. Compare any cash offer against a listing net, and ask what each route leaves you after liens and the documentary tax.

More questions about New Orleans, LA

Do I need to fix code violations before selling a house in New Orleans?

Not always, but open violations can lead to a hearing and a lien, and a lien must be paid or released at closing. Fixing the cited items before a hearing can end the case without further city action, according to the city's blight process.

Who pays the documentary transaction tax on a New Orleans sale?

The Orleans Parish Clerk's page names the seller among the parties responsible. The tax is a flat $325 for most documents, paid when the act is recorded.

Where do I record a deed or act of sale in New Orleans?

At the Land Records Division of the Orleans Parish Clerk of Civil District Court, 1340 Poydras Street, 4th Floor. It is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.

Can I sell a New Orleans house that has an unpermitted short term rental history?

Yes, but the city can pursue unpermitted rentals through adjudication, and permits do not transfer to a buyer. Resolve open cases and any unpaid taxes or liens first.

What if a New Orleans house is in an inherited succession?

Title still has to be sorted out before a sale. Because the code process researches every person with a legal interest in the property, unopened successions can slow a hearing or a sale, so talk to a Louisiana attorney or notary about the succession.

How is Baton Rouge organized, and why does that matter to a seller?

Baton Rouge is the Louisiana capital and the seat of East Baton Rouge Parish, and the city and parish run as one consolidated government. A house inside the city limits therefore deals with parish offices for permits, blight enforcement and recording.

The city sits on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River. According to its Wikipedia entry, the original draw was the Istrouma Bluff, the first natural bluff upriver from the Gulf, which gave early settlers a business quarter safe from seasonal flooding. The area was founded in 1699, settled in 1721 and incorporated on January 16, 1817.

The Census Bureau counted 227,470 residents in 2020 and lists 86.32 square miles of land. Greater Baton Rouge held 870,569 people that year, so the market around the city is far larger than the city itself.

Neighborhood names that come up often in sale conversations include Highland Road, the Garden District, Goodwood, Scotlandville, Mid-City and the Perkins Road area. Interstates 10, 12 and 110 connect them, and Baton Rouge Metropolitan Airport serves the region.

What do the Census numbers say about Baton Rouge housing?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures show a city where fewer than half of occupied homes are owner-occupied, with a median home value of $234,700. Those are survey medians for the whole city, not a value for any single house.

A rental share above 50 percent is why many Baton Rouge sellers are landlords. An owner with a tenant in place, a lease that runs past the sale date or a unit that sat vacant after a bad move-out has a different set of choices than an owner-occupant.

Source: Census Bureau QuickFacts for Baton Rouge.

How did the August 2016 flood change selling a house in Baton Rouge?

The August 2016 flood is the single event most buyers and lenders still ask about. NOAA describes 20 to 30 inches of rain over several days, more than 30,000 rescues and over 50,000 homes damaged or destroyed across southern Louisiana.

The Army Corps of Engineers gives a parish-level picture: about 109,000 homes flooded in Louisiana, with 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes. Its estimate of residential damage was $3.8 billion, of which $2.3 billion fell in those two parishes.

For a seller, that history has practical consequences:

  • Buyers and insurers will ask whether the house took water in 2016 and what repairs were permitted.
  • The Louisiana Real Estate Commission publishes a mandatory Property Disclosure form for 2026, so review it early and answer any water history questions with care.
  • Unpermitted repairs from that period can surface when a buyer pulls permit history.
  • Flood zone and elevation records can move a lender's appetite, which is a common reason financed sales fall through.

The Comite River Diversion, a 12-mile channel meant to cut headwater flooding in the area, is still being built. The Corps reports that all 23 contracts were awarded by the end of fiscal year 2025, with six under construction. Its completion date is not stated on the project page, so it is not a safe basis for assuming lower risk on a particular street.

Sources: NOAA NCEI, Army Corps Comite River Diversion page.

What does Baton Rouge code enforcement do about overgrown or neglected houses?

Baton Rouge treats weeds and brush that reach eight inches as a nuisance under the city-parish code. A property with a blight violation gets a notice giving the owner 15 days to fix it, plus a blight court date.

If the problem is still there at the hearing, the court can enter a judgment with a fine and costs. The Department of Development may then clear the property itself and place a lien for the cost. A lien like that stays with the land and has to be dealt with at closing.

  • Report a violation by calling 311.
  • Questions about a notice go to Neighborhood Improvement at 225-389-8680.
  • The Department of Development handles construction permits and code enforcement for the parish and can be reached at 225-389-3171.

The city also publishes a page on adjudicated property, which matters if an inherited house has a history of unpaid taxes. Owners of vacant or inherited houses often find out about a blight case only when a lien shows up in a title search. Checking the address with the city before listing avoids a surprise.

Source: City of Baton Rouge code enforcement FAQ.

How does a house sale actually close in East Baton Rouge Parish?

Under the Louisiana Civil Code, a sale or promise of sale of an immovable has to be made by authentic act or by act under private signature. An authentic act is signed before a notary and two witnesses, which is why Louisiana closings run through a notary.

The signed act of sale is then recorded with the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court, whose Recording Department keeps conveyance records indexed by vendee and vendor. Recording fees are due when the document is recorded. The Recording Department's phone is (225) 389-3985, and the mailing address is P.O. Box 1991, Baton Rouge, LA 70821-1991.

The Louisiana Real Estate Commission's 2026 mandatory forms, including the Property Disclosure and the Residential Agreement to Buy or Sell, took effect on January 1, 2026. Ask your closing professional which forms apply to your sale, and answer disclosure questions honestly either way.

Sources: Civil Code art. 2440, EBR Clerk of Court recording page, LREC 2026 forms notice.

What are the main ways to sell a Baton Rouge house, and what does each ask of the seller?

Sellers in Baton Rouge usually choose between a listing, a for-sale-by-owner sale and a cash sale to an investor. The right fit depends on the house's condition, the flood history and how fast the money is needed.

  • Listing with an agent: Best for a clean, repaired house where you can wait through showings and a buyer's financing and appraisal.
  • For sale by owner: You keep the agent's side of the work, including disclosure paperwork, buyer screening and coordination with the notary.
  • Cash sale as-is: Suits a house with flood damage, deferred repairs, a tenant or a blight notice, because the buyer is not relying on a lender's inspection.

Louisiana adopted a new law on wholesaling residential real estate in the 2026 session (Act 807). The Real Estate Commission has issued a mandatory cancellation notice under it and describes the law as adding disclosures and documentation to protect consumers. Whoever you sell to, ask whether the buyer intends to keep the house or assign the contract, and read any cancellation language before signing.

Source: Louisiana Real Estate Commission notice on Act 807.

Which employers and institutions drive Baton Rouge housing demand?

Baton Rouge is a capital, a university town and an industrial port, and each of those supports a different slice of the housing market. State government is one of the largest single employers, and Louisiana State University and Southern University anchor the north and south sides of the city.

ExxonMobil says it has operated in the Baton Rouge area for more than 115 years with a workforce of 6,000 people. The regional business group lists LSU as the second-largest employer in the region with more than 5,000 employees. The Port of Greater Baton Rouge ranks tenth in the country by tonnage and is the farthest upstream Mississippi River port that can handle Panamax ships.

The climate adds its own cost to ownership. Baton Rouge averages 61.94 inches of rain a year and a July average temperature of 83.0 degrees, and Hurricane Gustav brought winds over 100 miles per hour on September 1, 2008. Roofs, drainage and air conditioning age fast in that weather, and buyers price them in.

Sources: Wikipedia: Baton Rouge, ExxonMobil Baton Rouge operations, Better in BTR.

What should a Baton Rouge seller check before accepting an offer?

Start with the address itself: flood history, open code cases, permits and liens. Each can change what a buyer will pay or whether a lender will close.

  • Pull your flood zone and any 2016 water history so you can answer disclosure questions accurately.
  • Call 311 or Neighborhood Improvement to confirm there is no open blight case.
  • Ask a title company to search the conveyance and mortgage records for liens.
  • For an inherited house, confirm who has authority to sign before you accept anything.
  • Keep copies of repair invoices and permits from any post-2016 work.

Taking an hour on these steps usually saves weeks later, whichever route you choose.

More questions about Baton Rouge, LA

Do I need a notary to sell a house in Baton Rouge?

In practice, yes. Louisiana requires a sale of real estate to be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, and closings are normally signed before a notary and recorded with the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court. A title company or closing attorney usually arranges this.

Does a Baton Rouge house that flooded in 2016 have to be disclosed?

Buyers and insurers are likely to ask about it, and the Louisiana Real Estate Commission publishes a mandatory 2026 Property Disclosure form. Ask your closing professional how it applies to your sale, answer plainly and keep repair records.

What happens if my Baton Rouge house has a blight violation?

The owner gets a notice with 15 days to correct the problem and a blight court date. If it is not cleared, the court can assess a fine and costs, and the city can clear the property and place a lien. Call 311 or 225-389-8680 to ask about the status.

Where are Baton Rouge deeds recorded?

At the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court, Recording Department, which keeps conveyance records indexed by vendee and vendor. Fees are due when the document is recorded, and the department's phone number is (225) 389-3985.

How many Baton Rouge homes are owner-occupied?

The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied housing unit rate at 47.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, with a median owner-occupied home value of $234,700. Those figures describe the whole city, not a particular neighborhood or house.

Where is Shreveport, and how did it grow?

Shreveport is the parish seat of Caddo Parish in northwest Louisiana, on the west bank of the Red River, and part of it extends into Bossier Parish. The Shreve Town Company founded it in 1836 at the point where the newly navigable river met the Texas Trail, an overland route into the Republic of Texas (Wikipedia).

The city sits in the Ark-La-Tex area where Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas meet. The Census Bureau lists a total area of 123.396 square miles, of which 107.798 is land and 15.548 is water.

Oil built much of twentieth century Shreveport. Standard Oil of Louisiana and United Gas Corporation were headquartered here for decades, and the city later saw drilling activity return through the Haynesville Shale. The 2020 census counted 187,593 residents in the city and 393,406 in the Shreveport-Bossier City metro area.

What does the Shreveport climate mean for a roof and a yard?

Shreveport has a humid subtropical climate, with normal annual rainfall above 51 inches, and spring and summer bring severe thunderstorms with hail, damaging wind and tornadoes. Wikipedia reports average monthly rainfall from under 3 inches in August to more than 5 inches in June.

For a seller, that points to roofs, gutters and tree limbs. An older roof with hail marks or patched leaks is something a conventional buyer's inspector and insurer will flag, and a repair estimate can move a deal. A cash buyer looks at the same roof but prices the work in, so the repair is not a closing condition.

Who employs people in Shreveport and Bossier City?

Government, health care and education dominate. The local economic development group's major employers list covers the Shreveport-Bossier area, so the figures below include employers across the river.

Local colleges include Louisiana State University Shreveport, LSU Health Sciences Center Shreveport and Southern University at Shreveport. Employers of this size mean many households here depend on the base, the schools or the hospitals.

How do roads and transit shape Shreveport neighborhoods?

Interstate 20 runs across the area and the city has a loop layout. Interstate 220 forms the outer loop to the north, and Louisiana Highway 3132 is the inner loop to the south, together making a semicircle of about 8 miles in diameter around downtown.

The Long-Allen Bridge, also called the Texas Street Bridge, links Shreveport and Bossier City. Sportran runs 17 bus routes seven days a week, with service from 6:00 a.m. to 1:00 a.m. and no night service on Sunday. The city has a Regional Airport and a Downtown Airport. Check how far a house sits from the loop and the interstate when you compare it with nearby sales.

What does Shreveport Property Standards do about neglected houses?

The city's Department of Property Standards handles abatement of vacant, overgrown and unsafe property. A recent city legal notice published in October 2025 shows how the process works, and it is the clearest description of what a Shreveport owner faces.

  • Owners listed in the notice must fix care of premises, securing and inoperable vehicle violations within 10 days of publication, and demolitions within 30 days.
  • If an owner does not comply, the city can do the work with its own crews or a contractor, and the cost is the owner's responsibility.
  • The city adds an administrative charge of $500 on top of the work, and it may enforce a lien under its ordinance and state law.
  • Environmental Court fines run up to $75 per day per violation on residential property and $300 on commercial property, with a $5,000 cap for residential fines. Owners age 65 and older get an additional 30 days before enforcement.
  • A written appeal is due within 10 days of publication, sent to the Department of Property Standards at P. O. Box 31109, Shreveport, LA 71130.

The notice ends with a line that matters to any buyer: anyone acquiring an interest in a listed property is subject to its requirements. Many of the addresses in that notice are held by estates or unopened successions, which is the situation a lot of heirs here find themselves in. Read the full public notice to see the format.

How do Shreveport and Caddo Parish handle property tax at a sale?

Two bills may apply: one for the parish and one for the city's downtown district if the property sits in it. The Caddo Parish Assessor values the property. The city says that tax notices for the city and the Downtown Development Authority (Central Business District) go out in mid-November, with payment due December 31, collected by the City Finance Department (city page). The city lists the Caddo Parish Tax Assessor at 318-226-6701.

The Caddo Parish Sheriff collects parish taxes. Taxes are due by December 31, and the sheriff accepts mailed payments at PO Box 20905, Shreveport, LA 71120-0905, per its public notice page. At closing, expect the title company to prorate the year's bill, so ask early whether the current bill has been paid.

What does recording a sale in Caddo Parish cost?

The Caddo Parish Clerk records deeds, mortgages, rights of way, powers of attorney, judgments and tax liens. Its recording fee schedule sets conveyance and mortgage fees by page count.

The clerk's page also notes an additional $5 fee collected by the statewide records authority starting January 1, 2027. The record room can help locate a document but cannot do a title search, and the clerk has indexed conveyances back to 1914 and scanned them back to 1838.

When does a cash sale make sense in Shreveport?

The situations that tend to fit are an inherited house with open Property Standards notices, a vacant property with grass or securing violations, a house with roof or storm damage, or a rental with long-term tenant problems. In each case the owner wants a firm closing date and a buyer who will take the property as it is.

Title still has to be clear. Sort out any lien from a city abatement, any unpaid tax and any succession questions with a Louisiana notary or attorney before the act of sale. Compare a cash price against what a listing would net after repairs, carrying costs and commissions.

More questions about Shreveport, LA

How long do I have to fix a Shreveport property standards violation?

Under the city's October 2025 notice, owners had 10 days from publication for care of premises, securing and vehicle violations and 30 days for demolitions. Appeals are due within 10 days.

Can the City of Shreveport put a lien on my house?

Yes. If the city has to do the abatement work, the owner owes the cost plus a $500 administrative charge, and the city can enforce a lien under its ordinance and state law.

When are Caddo Parish property taxes due?

They are due by December 31 of the year assessed. City and downtown district notices are mailed in mid-November.

What does it cost to record a deed in Caddo Parish?

A conveyance of 1 to 5 pages is $105, 6 to 25 pages is $205, and 26 to 50 pages is $305, per the clerk's schedule. Fees can change, so confirm with the clerk.

Can heirs sell a Shreveport house before the succession is finished?

Title has to be established first. Talk to a Louisiana attorney or notary about whether a judgment of possession is needed before an act of sale can be signed.

Does hail damage hurt a Shreveport sale?

It can, since Shreveport sees hail and tornadoes in spring and summer. A cash buyer will price the damage into an offer, while a conventional buyer's inspector may request repairs.

Where is Bossier City, and how did it grow?

Bossier City sits in Bossier Parish on the eastern bank of the Red River, directly across from Shreveport. The two cities share one metro area, and Bossier City is the second-largest city in it.

Bossier Parish was created in 1843. According to Wikipedia's history of the city, the railroad boom of the 1880s brought the town to life: a golden spike completed the Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific Railroad here on July 12, 1884. The settlement of Cane City was incorporated in 1907 and renamed Bossier City. On June 23, 1925, a fire consumed about half of downtown, and construction on Barksdale Airfield began in the 1930s.

Today the Census Bureau counts 62,701 residents in 2020 and 63,259 in its July 1, 2025 estimate, spread across 43.80 square miles of land. Interstate 20, Interstate 220 and US Route 80 are the main roads, and Arthur Ray Teague Parkway and the Bossier Strip are common landmarks in listings.

What does the Census say about Bossier City homes and owners?

Bossier City is a closer split between owners and renters than the suburbs around it, with 53.2 percent of housing units owner-occupied. The Census Bureau puts the median owner-occupied home value at $202,100 for 2020 to 2024.

How much does Barksdale Air Force Base shape the Bossier City housing market?

Barksdale Air Force Base is the biggest single influence on housing turnover in Bossier City. The base is home to the 2d Bomb Wing, which the Air Force calls the largest bomb wing in the service, and it also houses Air Force Global Strike Command and Eighth Air Force.

The 2d Bomb Wing fact sheet says the base supports nearly 9,000 active-duty, Reserve and civilian workers plus 6,000 dependents, and that it maintains about 1,000 houses on base. It also reports a $980 million economic impact for 2023. The fiscal year 2024 economic impact statement lists a total payroll of $622,272,959 and a total economic impact of $1,112,534,993.

For sellers, military orders create two patterns:

  • Sellers on a short permanent change of station timeline who cannot wait for a buyer's financing.
  • Owners who moved away and now manage a rental from a distance, then decide to sell after a bad vacancy or repair bill.

Both groups tend to value a fixed closing date over a top-dollar listing, which is worth thinking about before choosing a route.

Sources: Barksdale 2d Bomb Wing fact sheet, FY 2024 economic impact statement.

What other employers and institutions anchor Bossier City?

Casinos, the Cyber Innovation Center and Bossier Parish Community College round out the local economy beyond the base. Riverboat casino resorts line the east bank of the Red River, including Margaritaville, Horseshoe and Boomtown, and Louisiana Downs has offered horse racing and slot machines since 1974.

The Cyber Innovation Center and its National Cyber Research Park host technology employers and research partners, including General Dynamics Information Technology. Bossier Parish Schools serve the city's students, and the parish operates its own community college.

Job mix matters for sellers because hospitality, defense and technology employers draw different kinds of buyers and tenants.

Sources: Wikipedia: Bossier City, Bossier Innovates.

What weather and flood risks do Bossier City homes face?

Bossier City has a humid climate with roughly 51 inches of rain a year, hot summers and the occasional hard freeze. Wikipedia's table for the Shreveport Regional Airport, the nearest long-record station, shows 51.41 inches of average precipitation, 101.2 days with measurable rain and 1.4 inches of snow a year.

The same table lists a record high of 110 degrees in August and a record low of minus 5 degrees in February. Air conditioning loads are heavy for months, and a freeze can crack exposed pipes, so a buyer's inspector will look closely at the HVAC system, the attic and any plumbing in unheated spaces.

  • Roofs and attic ventilation take a beating from the summer heat, so keep any roof invoices handy.
  • Homes near the Red River or its bayous should have a current flood zone determination ready.
  • Older houses may have galvanized plumbing or aging electrical panels that lenders flag.

Pulling the FEMA flood map for your parcel before you list gives you an answer to the first question most buyers ask.

What does Bossier City expect from property owners on maintenance?

Bossier City enforces basic maintenance standards on private property through its Property Standards and Code Enforcement Division. The city describes it as responsible for those standards, and its violations page asks residents to include as much detail as possible about an alleged violation.

Properties in unincorporated parts of the parish fall under a separate Property Standards department run by the Bossier Parish Police Jury, so the answer to who to call depends on whether an address is inside the city limits. The city's ordinances are posted in the Municode library, which is the place to confirm current rules.

An owner who has left a house vacant, especially after an inheritance, should walk the lot and check for overgrown grass, broken fencing and debris before listing. Clearing these items can prevent a complaint from turning into a lien or a delayed closing.

Sources: Bossier City Property Standards Division, Bossier Parish Police Jury Property Standards.

The best route depends on timing, condition and tenants. A listing can reach more buyers, while a cash sale usually moves faster and carries fewer repair demands.

  • An heir managing an out-of-state estate may want one signing rather than many showings.

No. Bossier City is a separate city in Bossier Parish on the eastern bank of the Red River, across from Shreveport in Caddo Parish. The two share one metro area and many employers.

The Bossier Parish Clerk of Court records conveyance and mortgage documents. The listed fee is $105 for one to five pages, which includes indexing up to 10 names, a certified copy and the portal fee.

The Property Standards and Code Enforcement Division enforces basic maintenance standards on private property inside the city. Unincorporated areas go to the Bossier Parish Police Jury's Property Standards department.

It can. The base supports nearly 9,000 workers and had a reported $980 million economic impact in 2023, so military moves create regular turnover. Sellers on orders often care most about a dependable closing date.

Wikipedia lists the city as founded in the 1830s, incorporated in 1848 and reincorporated in 1898. It is the principal city of the Houma-Bayou Cane-Thibodaux metropolitan area. Hurricane Ida made landfall in southeast Louisiana on August 29, 2021, and Houma took the intense eye wall of the Category 4 storm. Wikipedia describes widespread damage, and a year later NBC News reported displacement and property damage still lingering.

FEMA's one-year summary gives the statewide scale: more than 564,000 individual assistance applications approved for over $1.2 billion, 14,540 flood insurance claims paid for more than $655 million and over 26,000 Small Business Administration disaster loan applications. For a seller whose house was hit, buyers tend to ask:

  • Was there wind-driven water inside the walls or attic?
  • Did an insurance or FEMA payment cover the repairs, and were the repairs finished?
  • Are there leftover blue tarps, rotted decking or mold?

An as-is buyer who does not need a lender's appraisal can often close despite open repairs, which is why damaged houses sometimes sell this way.

Preliminary maps are not final, so check the status for your address before telling a buyer what zone it is in. A seller can do three things:

Houma's economy rests on energy, marine work, seafood and health care. The Terrebonne Parish Economic Development Authority calls the parish one of the leading regions for oil and gas production in the country, and says that industry sustains a large inland marine and port economy.

It also describes Terrebonne as a leader in shrimp, oyster and other aquaculture harvesting, with a significant base of sugar cane farming. Aviation supports about 750 jobs, plus 2,000 direct industrial jobs at the airport's industrial park, and health services employ about 7,000.

Energy employment moves with oil prices and offshore activity, which can leave a household with a house to sell on short notice after a layoff or a transfer. A buyer who can close on a firm date is useful in that situation.

According to Wikipedia, businessman Russell Starns led the effort, which grew out of a wish to have a school system separate from East Baton Rouge Parish's. The Legislature allowed a separate system only after the city incorporated. Central had about 25,000 residents at the time, and residents are zoned to the Central Community School System.

For a seller, the practical point is that permits, planning and floodplain questions go to Central City Hall at 11530 Sullivan Road, phone 225.262.5000. Recording of the deed, however, still happens at the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court because Central sits inside that parish.

Where is Central, and what is the land like?

Central is in the east-central part of East Baton Rouge Parish, between the Comite River on its west border and the Amite River, which forms the line with Livingston Parish. The two rivers meet near the city's southern edge.

The Census Bureau lists 62.26 square miles of land, which makes Central far larger in area than its population suggests. Louisiana Highway 408 runs through the center and leads about 7 miles west to Interstate 110 in north Baton Rouge. Louisiana Highway 37 crosses the eastern side. Downtown Baton Rouge is about 13 miles southwest.

How did the 2016 flood affect Central?

Central was one of the hardest-hit parts of East Baton Rouge Parish in August 2016. WAFB reported significant flooding, and Mayor Jr. Shelton said the number of Central residents affected was 25,000.

The Army Corps of Engineers says the August 2016 flood far exceeded the flood of record in the Comite River basin, with about 109,000 homes flooded across Louisiana and 79,000 of them in East Baton Rouge and Livingston Parishes. The Comite River Diversion is the project meant to reduce headwater flooding on this side of the parish. It can also state whether the property is in a repetitive loss area and the 2016 flood depth at the property. For a seller, that last item answers the most common buyer question with an official number instead of a rumor.

  • The city keeps elevation certificates on file for structures completed after 2008 and publishes a list of those properties.
  • An owner whose elevation certificate shows the structure is above the flood level may qualify to seek removal from the floodplain through a Letter of Map Change.
  • Central takes part in the Community Rating System, which can lower flood insurance premiums for policy holders.

Ordering the determination before you list takes one question off the table and gives a buyer's lender a document to work from.

What permits does Central require, and when do repairs need one?

Central requires permits for most work beyond cosmetic touch-ups, including remodels, additions, roofing, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work, fences, generators and demolitions. Accessory buildings over 200 square feet and portable structures over 120 square feet also need a permit.

A separate disturbance permit is required before using mechanized equipment to disturb land, remove trees by machine, haul in more than 12 cubic yards of soil, sand or fill, or demolish a structure with heavy equipment. The floodplain manager may approve up to 12 inches of fill without a geotechnical report. Anything deeper needs engineered lifts, a geotechnical report and a topography plan by a licensed civil engineer, and it must not harm drainage on neighboring land.

The Permit Desk can be reached at 225.262.5000, extension 1. The city has also dropped its separate trade contractor license as a prerequisite for permit approval.

This matters at sale time. If you raised a yard, added a carport or replaced a roof without a permit, a buyer's inspector or lender may flag it. Unpermitted work is easier to fix before an offer than after.

How does a sale close in Central, and which route fits?

A Central sale closes the same way as any Louisiana sale. The Civil Code requires a sale of an immovable to be made by authentic act or by act under private signature, so you sign before a notary and the act is recorded with the East Baton Rouge Parish Clerk of Court.

That clerk's Recording Department can be reached at (225) 389-3985, and fees are due when a document is recorded. The Louisiana Real Estate Commission's 2026 mandatory forms, including the Property Disclosure, took effect on January 1, 2026.

No. Central is its own city, incorporated on April 23, 2005, though it lies in East Baton Rouge Parish and belongs to the Baton Rouge metro area. It has its own city government and its own school system.

Where is Slidell, and how did it start?

Slidell is a city on the northeast shore of Lake Pontchartrain in St. Tammany Parish, and it belongs to the New Orleans metropolitan area. The 2020 census counted 28,781 residents, which made it the 16th most populous city in Louisiana (Wikipedia).

The town grew up during construction of the New Orleans and Northeastern Railroad in 1882 and 1883, a line that tied New Orleans to Meridian, Mississippi. It was named for John Slidell and chartered by the legislature in 1888. Its official nickname is the Camellia City.

The city covers 15.2 square miles, and only 2.39 percent of that is water. Gause Boulevard, a major east-west street, started as the path between a lumber yard and a log cabin built by an early settler family.

What shaped Slidell's economy?

Federal science and defense work did, along with the interstates. In the 1960s NASA opened the Michoud Assembly Facility in New Orleans and the Stennis Space Center in Hancock County, Mississippi, and put a computer center on Gause Boulevard. Wikipedia says this nearly tripled Slidell's population in ten years and turned it into a major New Orleans suburb.

The National Weather Service forecast office for the New Orleans and Baton Rouge area is in Slidell. Textron Marine and Land Systems has its global headquarters off Gause Boulevard. Interstates 10, 59 and 12 meet in the area, which made Slidell a crossroads for traffic across the Gulf states.

How does flooding affect a Slidell house sale?

Flood risk is the first question most Slidell buyers and lenders ask. The city's Flood Safety brochure says Slidell is subject to flooding from hurricane storm surge, back flooding of Bayou Bonfouca when Lake Pontchartrain is inundated, and local drainage problems during heavy storms. It adds that flooding can occur in any season and that, because much of the land is low and flat, all properties are potentially at risk.

Hurricane Katrina is the reference point. The municipal area is about 2 miles inland, yet parts of the city saw storm surge above 10 feet on August 29, 2005. Unincorporated areas of St. Tammany to the south and east that often carry a Slidell address saw 13 to 16 feet.

A seller can prepare by finding the flood zone before listing. The brochure says to ask the city's Floodplain Administrator in the Building Safety Department, which can also advise on whether a property is prone to flooding.

What do Slidell rules on permits and repairs mean for sellers?

Slidell has a flood hazard prevention ordinance that meets National Flood Insurance Program standards. A permit is required for any development, which the brochure defines to include new construction, substantial improvements, demolitions and excavations. It also warns that anyone who fills, dumps or excavates land or drainage ways without permission can be ordered to restore it at their own cost.

  • Planning Department: 985-646-4320, at 250 Bouscaren St, Suite 203, Slidell, LA 70458.
  • Building Safety Department: 985-646-4323.
  • Engineering Department: 985-646-4270.
  • Code Enforcement: 985-646-6134.

These numbers come from a brochure dated March 2020, so confirm them with the city. If you are planning repairs before a sale, ask whether the work will count as a substantial improvement, and whether a drainage or fill change needs engineering review.

Why does flood insurance timing matter when selling in Slidell?

Standard property insurance does not cover surface flooding, so a separate National Flood Insurance Program policy is needed. The city advises that new flood policies usually have a 30 day waiting period and that no new policy can start once a named storm has formed in or entered the Gulf of Mexico.

The brochure makes one helpful point for buyers: if you buy a new home, the 30 day waiting period does not apply, and coverage starts once the application is approved after closing. A seller can help a buyer by having the property's flood zone and any prior claims ready early.

The city also describes federal grants for repetitive loss properties. Repetitive loss means two or more NFIP claims over $1,000 each within a rolling ten years. Severe repetitive loss has stricter tests, and grants can pay for elevation, acquisition or demolition. Ask the Finance Department about them if your house flooded more than once.

The St. Tammany Parish Sheriff does, for Slidell as well as the unincorporated parish. Under Louisiana law the sheriff in each parish collects property taxes, and the sheriff's Property Tax Division collects for Slidell, Mandeville, Covington, Abita Springs, Pearl River and Madisonville under separate contract, per the sheriff's property tax page.

The St. Tammany Parish Clerk of Court records conveyance, mortgage and miscellaneous documents about immovable property for the entire parish, through its Recording Department. The clerk posts a 2026 fee schedule as a PDF, and the main number for the office is 985-809-8700.

Louisiana sales are passed before a notary. A title company or notary usually takes the signed act of sale to the clerk and pays the recording fee from closing funds.

Which schools serve Slidell?

St. Tammany Parish Public Schools runs the city's public schools, and its three Slidell high schools are Northshore High School, Salmen High School and Slidell High School. Buyers often ask which zone a house falls in, so confirm attendance boundaries with the district rather than relying on a listing description.

What must a Slidell seller disclose about the house?

Louisiana law asks sellers of residential property to complete a property disclosure document. R.S. 9:3198 says the seller must use a form prescribed by the Louisiana Real Estate Commission or one with at least its minimum language (Justia copy of the statute). In a place with Slidell's flood history, that form is where past water damage and repairs belong.

Slidell has a humid subtropical climate, with short, mild winters and hot, humid summers, and Wikipedia notes that hurricanes pose a threat because of the low elevation. Old repairs, mold and missing records can slow a conventional sale, which is another reason some owners look at a cash offer.

When does a cash sale fit a Slidell house?

It tends to fit a house with flood damage that has not been repaired, a house with a lapsed flood policy, an estate property or a rental the owner no longer wants. A cash buyer takes the property as it stands, so a lender's appraisal and repair demands are not part of the deal. Title work, tax certificates and recording still apply.

Parts of it are. The city says all properties are potentially at risk because the land is low and flat. Call the Floodplain Administrator in Building Safety at 985-646-4323 to learn a specific property's zone.

Slidell requires a permit for any development, including substantial improvements and demolitions. Ask Building Safety before starting work.

Who do I pay Slidell property taxes to?

The St. Tammany Parish Sheriff's Property Tax Division collects them for Slidell under contract. You can call 985-809-8217.

The city's brochure says the 30 day waiting period does not apply when you buy a new home. Coverage starts after the application is approved following closing.

At the St. Tammany Parish Clerk of Court, Recording Department. The clerk handles conveyances and mortgages for the whole parish.

Yes. Conventional buyers may ask for repairs or walk away, while a cash buyer can offer on the house as it stands. Clear title and tax status are still needed.

The city dates its founding to the spring of 1779, when about 500 colonists from Spain, led by Lieutenant Colonel Francisco Bouligny, came up Bayou Teche and settled near what became Spanish Lake. The settlers called the town Nueva Iberia after the Iberian Peninsula.

The city covers 10.6 square miles, all of it land, and lies roughly 16 to 20 feet above mean sea level. Lake Peigneur and Spanish Lake are among the water bodies nearby.

What does the economy of New Iberia rest on?

Agriculture, small business and food and manufacturing brands. Sugar cane is a principal crop for local farmers, and the Louisiana Sugar Cane Festival each September marks the start of the harvest, which locals call grinding.

Avery Island, famous for Tabasco sauce, rock salt deposits and Jungle Gardens, is part of the area. Trappey's Hot Sauce was born in New Iberia, and Louisiana Hot Sauce, Acadiana Regional Airport and the Amtrak station are named as parts of the local economy. Shadows-on-the-Teche, owned by the National Trust for Historic Preservation, and the Bayou Teche Museum draw visitors to the downtown area.

How do roads and travel work around New Iberia?

U.S. 90 is the main four-lane highway and is designated as future Interstate 49. Acadiana Regional Airport is a general aviation field, and scheduled passenger service is at Lafayette Regional Airport, which sits next to U.S. 90 in Lafayette. Amtrak's Sunset Limited, running between Los Angeles and New Orleans, serves the city.

The nearest airline service is in Lafayette, which is part of the same metropolitan area, so access to U.S. 90 is a fair point to raise when you describe a house.

New Iberia has a subtropical climate with above-average rainfall. As of 2021 the annual average high was 79.1 degrees and the average low was 59.4 degrees. Wikipedia also shows flooding in the city from Hurricane Ike in September 2008.

Flood history, roof age and drainage are the three things a buyer's insurer will likely ask about. Pull any past claims and repair receipts before a sale, because gaps in paperwork slow a conventional closing more than the repairs themselves.

The city's Compliance and Right-of-Way Office does. Its page says the compliance officer works with all departments to enforce ordinances, especially condemnation of houses, grass, abandoned vehicles and junk.
